title: Consulting doctors and Dr. Mayer's diagnosis of Pott's disease
summary: Cobb gets a second opinion; Dr. Mayer, with agent Ben Barth present, diagnoses Pott's disease and warns of nine months in bed.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: So I knew I had to tell my agent; I had to call him from somewhere, so I opened up and told them. Then I called my agent, and he was the man who suggested (unintelligible) and he said, "Are you sure?" And I said, "I'll tell you what the man said." So we had a consultation -- I spent $85 and went to a Doctor Shine for $35 on Fifth Avenue, and went to Dr. Leo B. Mayer on Madison Avenue, who was President Roosevelt's doctor, but it was hard for me to get to see him, but through the office, there was a secretary in there that knew somebody in the office that could talk to him, and you know, everything, you know, you have influence with one or two people and it's good -- it ain't what you know, it's who you know.
And the man was getting ready to go to Israel to set up a clinic, and he called the hospital and had me put in on a Thursday, and he operated on me on Monday -- the
day he was supposed to go to Israel and that Tuesday, the next day, he left after the operation was over.

But in his office, before I went in the hospital; four of us were in there; Ben Barth, my agent; my wife; Dr. Mayer; and myself. He gave me the rundown; he told me, he said, "You're not in your teens any more." I was 29 years old then. He said, "You got a bone condition, which is Pott's disease." That's what I was operated on for, which is the [Tuberculous] curvature of a bone and the only way you can get this, you got to get a heavy blow, a lick.
